title: The Dragon Cost Problem

topics.value_lesson: Being wrong on purpose is how things get made — a broken version is not a failure, it is the work

spine: A kid tries to build their first real board game, and the only way forward is through every version that breaks.

designer_name.role: The kid designer, the child in the story

friend_name.role: The skeptical best friend and keeper of Sir Bouncesalot

segments.text:
The argument lasted an entire rainy afternoon at the library chess club. Should a dragon cost five coins or six? Voices got louder. Someone knocked over a bishop. And that was when {designer_name} stood up on a chair and shouted the words that changed everything: we could just MAKE one.

That night, at the kitchen table, {designer_name} cut a cereal box flat and borrowed dice from three other games. The idea felt enormous in their head, a whole treasure island, players racing across it, coins to spend, a dragon at the far end. But when they picked up the pencil to write the first rule, the island turned to fog. The pencil hovered. Nothing came.

The doorbell rang. It was {friend_name}, rain on their hood, holding something small and battered between two fingers.

Sir Bouncesalot. The d20. The luckiest die in the world, if you asked {friend_name}, which nobody ever did.

They placed it on the table with great ceremony, like a knight laying down a sword, and looked at the blank cardboard.

A dragon to be slain, they said.

{designer_name} laughed, and something loosened. Okay, they said. Okay. What do we actually need?

{friend_name} rolled Sir Bouncesalot across the cereal box, because of course they did. Twenty. A good omen, obviously.

So they started with what they knew. Players need something to want. The treasure. Write it down. Players need a choice, a real one, not a fake one. Spend coins to move fast, or save them for the dragon, or buy a little luck. Write it down. And every choice needs a consequence, or nobody cares about anything. Write it down.

Goal, choice, consequence. Around and around.

They did not know it yet, but they had just built the thing that lives inside every game ever made. The loop. The engine.

{designer_name} drew a small star in the corner of the cardboard. It came out lopsided.

Version one, they said.

{friend_name} picked up Sir Bouncesalot and held it high. Then let the quest begin.

Play it, said {designer_name}. Obviously. We have to know.

{friend_name} grinned and grabbed the phone. Twenty minutes later Zara from chess club was sitting at the kitchen table, turning a cardboard coin over in her fingers, looking at the hand-drawn island the way a dragon looks at a sheep.

I'll go first, she said.

Zara did not move toward the treasure. Zara did not buy luck. Zara bought the dragon card. Every single round, she bought the dragon card, and every single round it stomped across the board and ate whatever the rest of them had built. On turn six, {friend_name} rolled Sir Bouncesalot with full ceremony, both hands, eyes closed, a small hum of destiny. Three. Zara's dragon ate their last coin anyway.

Eleven minutes after it started, it was over.

Zara pushed back her chair, and she said it kindly, which somehow made it worse. This part is boring. And also, I won without trying.

The kitchen went very quiet. Sir Bouncesalot sat on the table showing his three like a small bad moon.

{friend_name} picked him up and rolled him again, gently, as if apologizing. Six. Also bad.

Okay, said {designer_name}. Their ears were hot. Okay. Let's think.

They stared at the board. The treasure path. The luck cards. The dragon, sitting there at the far end, fat and smug, the best thing on the island by a mile.

Wait, said {designer_name} slowly. The problem isn't that the dragon is strong.

{friend_name} looked up.

The problem is that nothing else gives you a reason not to take it. Moving fast is worse. Luck is worse. Saving is worse. It's not a choice at all. It's just a door with one handle.

Zara leaned back in. Huh, she said. That's true. I never even read the other cards.

{designer_name} flipped the cereal box over and picked up the pencil. The first star, the lopsided one, was on the other side now, hidden against the table. They drew a new one in the fresh corner. It came out a little straighter.

Version two, they said.

{friend_name} lifted Sir Bouncesalot high. The quest continues.

Ask around, said {designer_name}. If we're wrong, I want to know before Zara does.

So the next morning, before anyone rolled anything, {designer_name} tucked the notebook under one arm and biked to the library, {friend_name} rattling alongside with Sir Bouncesalot in a jacket pocket like a tiny knight in a carriage.

The librarian listened to the whole thing. The island, the coins, the dragon. She did not fix anything. She just asked one question.

What do you want players to feel, right here? And she tapped the page where the dragon card was drawn.

{designer_name} opened their mouth and nothing came out. Nobody had asked that. They had argued about five coins or six for an entire afternoon and nobody had once asked that.

The librarian pulled a book off the shelf and found a picture of a seesaw. A game is balanced like this, she said. A beginner should beat an expert sometimes. Not always. Sometimes. If the expert always wins, the beginner quits. If it's pure luck, the expert quits. You're building the middle.

Then she told them about a man named Reiner Knizia, who has made hundreds of games, more than almost anyone alive, and who still builds every single one out of cardboard first. Ugly first versions, she said. On purpose. Cardboard is where games go to tell the truth.

{friend_name} leaned over the book. Hundreds, they whispered. And he still tests them. Like quests.

They biked home fast. The notebook felt heavier than before, in a good way, like a tool instead of a diary.

That afternoon they played version one anyway, just the two of them, because now they wanted to see it break. And it broke. {friend_name} played the Zara strategy, dragon card every round, and the game folded in eleven minutes flat. Sir Bouncesalot rolled twenty twice and it changed nothing, which {friend_name} took as a personal insult.

But this time {designer_name} was watching the seesaw. Every round, the dragon side just sat on the ground. Nothing weighed anything against it.

There, said {designer_name}. That's the wobble. It's not that the dragon is strong. It's that nothing else is a reason.

{friend_name} nodded slowly, then flipped the cereal box over. New corner. Fresh cardboard.

{designer_name} drew the star again. Straighter this time. You could tell what it was now.

Version two, they said.

{friend_name} raised Sir Bouncesalot like a banner. The quest continues.

Back at the kitchen table, {designer_name} stared at the lopsided star in the corner of the cardboard. Version one had wobbled. It had creaked. And somewhere in the middle of all that wobbling, a strange idea had landed: maybe it was supposed to.

"You know what?" {designer_name} said slowly. "I think version one was meant to be terrible. That's not failure. That's the job."

{friend_name} looked up from Sir Bouncesalot. "Say that again."

"Designers call it iteration. You build a version, you watch it break, you fix the thing that broke, and you build it again. Great games go through hundreds of versions. Hundreds."

{friend_name} was quiet for a moment. Then they picked up the pencil and pressed it into {designer_name}'s hand.

"Then stop talking," they said, "and iterate."

So they did. They crossed out the dragon's price and wrote something new: the dragon costs more every time someone buys it. First player pays five. Second pays seven. Third pays nine. Suddenly the dragon was not a shopping trip. It was a decision.

"And this," {designer_name} said, drawing a new card with a flourish, "is the lucky map. If you're losing, really losing, you can spend your last coins on a shortcut through the jungle. Might work. Might not."

{friend_name} grinned. "Skill for the expert. A real chance for the beginner."

"Balance," {designer_name} said, and the word felt like a key turning.

They redrew the star. Still a little wobbly. But better. Definitely better.

Version two.

{friend_name} lifted Sir Bouncesalot high, closed their eyes, and rolled with the ceremony of a knight anointing a battlefield. The die clattered across the cardboard.

They played. The loop turned. Goal, choice, consequence, around and around, and this time the game had a heartbeat. It was not perfect. Something still snagged near the end, something {designer_name} could not quite name yet.

But when the last coin was spent and the dragon finally fell, {friend_name} looked up with wide eyes and said the only word that matters in game design.

"Again."

"Luck," {designer_name} said. "We tip it toward luck."

{friend_name} stood up so fast their chair wobbled. "At last," they said, lifting Sir Bouncesalot to the light like a chalice. "The die has been waiting for this moment."

So version three grew chances the way a garden grows weeds. The lucky-map deck got fatter — shortcuts, rainstorms, a monkey who steals coins and sometimes gives them back wearing a tiny hat. {designer_name} added a weather die. Roll it at the start of each round: sun means everyone moves fast, wind means the boats drift, and rain means the dragon stays home and naps.

"Rain," {friend_name} breathed, reading the new card. "The dragon naps. That's beautiful."

Then came the playtest that nobody saw coming. {friend_name}'s mum wandered in for a cup of tea, got handed the dragon piece, and stayed. She had never played a board game in her life. She asked what the coins were for twice. She moved her boat the wrong way and apologised to it.

And she won.

Not by accident — by weather. Rain, rain, rain, three rounds running, and while Zara's brilliant plans drowned in puddles, Mum's little boat drifted straight into the harbour on a lucky map she'd drawn by pure fluke.

Zara put her face in her hands. "I have been defeated," she said, "by a nap."

But here is the thing {designer_name} noticed, scribbling in the notebook: Mum never once asked what the rules meant. The weather die explained itself. The lucky map explained itself. The game made sense to someone who had never played anything — and she still had to earn it, coin by coin, roll by roll.

"One more," Zara said.

They played three rounds. Nobody stopped saying it. One more. One more.

Late that night, {designer_name} redrew the star in the corner of the rules card. Straighter. Brighter. Almost perfect.

Version four, they wrote.

The storyteller still has that card. And tucked inside the notebook, drawn better every single time, is the star — proof that the best games are the ones where anyone at the table can win, on any given night, if the rain falls just right.

"Skill," {designer_name} said. "We tip it toward skill."

{friend_name} looked down at Sir Bouncesalot, cradled in their palm. "You hear that?" they whispered to the die. "She thinks she doesn't need you." They rolled it anyway, for luck, because some habits are sacred.

So version three sharpened its teeth. Coins could be saved across rounds now — hoard them, spend them later, feel clever. And the dragon? The dragon could be baited. Leave a trail of coins leading away from the treasure, and the greedy old thing would follow it, sniffing, while you slipped in the back way.

Zara's eyes went very bright.

It took her four turns. Four. She saved coins in rounds one and two, bought nothing, let everyone think she was floundering. Then in round three she laid a coin trail like breadcrumbs, sent the dragon waddling off toward the far beach, and strolled into the hoard with her pockets empty and her smile enormous.

"Three-turn trap," she said, leaning back. "I planned it before you finished shuffling."

{designer_name} stared at the board. Then at the rules. Then at Zara.

"That's brilliant," they said. "That's — wait. If you can do that, a new player will never win. Ever."

Zara's smile faded. She looked at the coin trail, at the dragon, at the hoard. "Oh," she said. "Oh no. I broke my own favourite game."

They fixed it together. One small rule: the first time you play, the dragon likes you. It starts one step closer to your boat. A soft landing. A welcome.

The final playtest ran long past dinner. Nobody noticed. Every choice mattered now — every coin, every turn, every risk — and even the players who were losing leaned forward, elbows on the table, watching the board like it might tell them a secret.

The storyteller still has the notebook. On the last page, under RULES, version four, someone has written in hopeful pencil: version five ideas.

The star in the corner is drawn better than ever. But there is room, still, for it to grow.

choice_points.question: "Right," says {friend_name}, slamming Sir Bouncesalot onto the table like a gauntlet. "The rules exist. Do we play this beautiful disaster right now and watch it burn, or do we sneak it past someone who actually knows games first?"

options.label: Test version one immediately and let it fall apart
Take the rules to the game librarian before anyone plays

choice_points.question: "Okay, version three needs a soul," {designer_name} says, tapping the pencil. "Zara wins every time she thinks, and your mum wins every time she's lucky. Which way do we tip the seesaw — more luck, so anyone can win? Or more skill, so outsmarting someone feels amazing?"

options.label: Grow the lucky-map deck and let dice shake the island
Add saving, baiting, and long plans for clever players

gathered_but_unused: Every game you love runs on the same invisible loop: there's a goal, you make a choice, something happens as a result, and then you want to go again. Designers call this the game loop, and it's the heartbeat of everything from tag to chess to Mario Kart.

Board game designer Reiner Knizia has made over 600 published games, and he still builds every new idea out of paper and cardboard first, testing it with real people before a single piece gets printed.

The game of Monopoly was originally invented in 1903 by a woman named Elizabeth Magie, and she called it The Landlord's Game. She designed it to show how unfair it felt when one person owned everything — the game itself was her argument.

When designers say a game needs 'balance,' they mean nobody should be able to win just by being lucky, and nobody should be able to win every single time just by being skilled. The sweet spot is a game where a beginner can sometimes beat an expert — but not always.

The first version of almost every great game is terrible. Designers expect this. They call each new version an 'iteration,' and some video games go through hundreds of iterations before anyone outside the studio ever plays them.

Shigeru Miyamoto, who created Mario, designed the very first level of Super Mario Bros. so that the first thing you see is a question block and a slow-moving mushroom — the level teaches you the rules before you've read a single word.

Playtesting is a real job. Game studios pay people — including kids your age, sometimes — to play unfinished games and say out loud exactly where they got confused, bored, or frustrated. Getting confused is the most useful thing a playtester can do.

The game of rock-paper-scissors is perfectly balanced — each choice beats one and loses to one — and yet mathematicians have studied it for decades because real humans are so bad at choosing randomly that patterns always sneak in.
